text: That is the quiet thing to carry forward out of all the dates and deals.
Before there was a University of Chicago on this ground, before any of the later fights over who belonged where, a single developer with a satchel and a borrowed name had already drawn the lines.
The trains made the land reachable.
And the pricing decided who got to live near the water and who did not.
Paul Cornell bought a stretch of empty lakefront in 1853 and bet that he could sell distance and exclusivity to a crowded city.
He won the bet, and he died a rich and honored man in 1904, buried out at Oak Woods on the South Side he had spent his life building.
The shape of that win is still under our feet.
